title: Day 41 · Week 5, Day 6 — Myths: bad sickness means a girl, sickness means a healthy pregnancy, and nothing can be done about it
summary: The second Myths episode, on the last day of Week 5. Your baby is 3–6 mm at the turn to Carnegie stage 13: the neural tube now closed at both ends, arm paddles, leg buds appearing, the heart starting to divide. Myth one, 'she's that sick, it's a girl' — half right: hyperemesis admissions carry higher odds of a girl (Schiff 2004, 2,110 admissions, OR 1.5; Veenendaal 2011 meta-analysis OR 1.27; Askling 1999), and in 91,666 Japanese pregnancies (Mitsuda 2019) the women with severe sickness had girls 54.1% of the time against 45.2% in the women with none and 48.7% overall — a real population effect and a useless test, five points off a coin. Myth two, 'sickness means a healthy pregnancy' — true on average and false as a sign: in 797 women with every loss counted from the hormone test, nausea halved the hazard of loss and vomiting quartered it (Hinkle 2016, JAMA Intern Med; Koren 2014 review), but a fifth of women with normal live births had no symptoms at all (Gadsby 1993; Lacroix 2000; 17% in JECS), the sickness stops in everyone and stops unevenly (mean cessation Day 84; half relieved by 14 weeks), and at the severe end the association flips to lower birth weight (OR 1.42), SGA (1.28) and preterm birth (1.32); the real signals are the physical ones from Days 28 and 38. Myth three, 'nothing can be done', in three forms: 'it's in her head' (Fairweather 1968 versus Fejzo 2024 in Nature — GDF15 from the feto-placental unit acting on her brainstem, β-thalassaemia women barely sick); 'ride it out' (Cochrane 2015's 'no high-quality evidence' is not 'ineffective'; ACOG PB 189 and RCOG GTG 69 make B6 ± doxylamine first-line and say early treatment may prevent hospital; ginger for nausea in 12 RCTs; thiamine before glucose, with 82 published cases of Wernicke's after a mean 6.6 weeks of vomiting); and 'the medicines are dangerous' (Bendectin, 33 million pregnancies, RR 0.95 for malformations across 27 studies, withdrawn in 1983 over lawsuits, after which admissions for vomiting in pregnancy rose 37% and then 50% per 1,000 births with no fall in malformations — Neutel & Johansen 1995). An emerging footnote on prevention via GDF15 desensitisation (Sharma 2025), labelled as such. Three sentences for the father to say, and the first PUQE score.
action: Tonight, three sentences and one score. The sentences are yours to say so she doesn't have to: to 'it must be a girl' — 'slightly more likely, and a coin would do about as well'; to 'at least it means the baby's healthy' — 'on average, it's not a test, and when it's bad it costs her'; to 'nothing can be done' — 'B6 and doxylamine, first-line in both guidelines, and we have the plan'. Then run the PUQE from Day 37 with her for the first time — hours of nausea, vomits, retches, each scored 1–5 — and write the total and the date in the pregnancy file. If it is 7 or more, question five on yesterday's list moves from the first visit to a phone call to the practice tomorrow morning.
